scope: Micropayments and payment channels (x402 and MPP lineage)
Card payment security (TAP and Agent Pay context)
Protocol analyses and recent papers (part c additions)

entries.title: zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models
entries.summary: Presents zkLLM, a zero-knowledge proof system specialized for large language model inference, with a parallel lookup argument for non-arithmetic tensor operations and a dedicated proof for attention. It lets a model owner prove that an output came from committed parameters without revealing them.
entries.whyItMatters: ERC-8004 leaves room for validators that check agent work with cryptographic proofs; zkLLM shows what a zkML validation response could attest to and how costly that proof is for transformer models.

entries.title: Scaling up Trustless DNN Inference with Zero-Knowledge Proofs
entries.summary: Builds the first ZK-SNARK proof of correct inference for a full-resolution ImageNet model, so a client can check after the fact that a machine learning service ran the promised model. It also sketches protocols that use these proofs to verify model accuracy and to pay for verified predictions.
entries.whyItMatters: An early, concrete answer to the question an ERC-8004 validator asks: did the service actually run the model it claimed, and can that be checked without trusting the server.

entries.title: Intel SGX Explained
entries.summary: A long technical analysis of Intel Software Guard Extensions built from Intel papers, manuals, a tutorial and patents. It explains enclave creation, memory protection and remote attestation, and it catalogs the side-channel and design weaknesses that limit the trust these guarantees deserve.
entries.whyItMatters: TEE attestation is one of the validation methods ERC-8004 anticipates; this paper is the standard reference for what an SGX attestation proves and where it does not hold.

entries.title: opML: Optimistic Machine Learning on Blockchain
entries.summary: Proposes opML, which runs machine learning inference for blockchains under an optimistic model: results are accepted unless a challenger wins an interactive fraud-proof game, similar to optimistic rollups. The authors argue this is far cheaper than zero-knowledge proofs and can serve large models on ordinary hardware.
entries.whyItMatters: Shows the crypto-economic alternative to zkML for ERC-8004 validation, where validators stake on a result and disputes, not proofs, keep inference honest.

entries.title: The Millicent Protocol for Inexpensive Electronic Commerce
entries.venue: Fourth International World Wide Web Conference (WWW4)
entries.summary: Describes Millicent, a protocol for web purchases below one cent in which brokers sell vendor-specific scrip that each vendor can validate locally, without extra network round trips or heavy cryptography. Brokers handle accounts and billing so vendors and customers do not need direct financial relationships.
entries.whyItMatters: The direct ancestor of pay-per-request web payments: x402 and MPP revisit the same goal of charging tiny amounts per HTTP resource, with stablecoins and facilitators in the broker role.

entries.title: PayWord and MicroMint: Two simple micropayment schemes
entries.summary: Introduces two micropayment schemes: PayWord, where a user commits to a hash chain and pays by revealing successive hash values, and MicroMint, where coins are hash collisions that are cheap to verify but costly to mint at scale. Both aim to make each payment far cheaper than a public-key signature.
entries.whyItMatters: The hash-chain idea behind PayWord is the template for streaming and session payments; MPP sessions and payment channels used with x402 apply the same principle of one setup and many cheap increments.

entries.title: Electronic lottery tickets as micropayments
entries.summary: Proposes paying for many small items with electronic lottery tickets: each ticket wins a larger payment with small probability, so the expected value equals the price while the number of real transactions drops sharply.
entries.whyItMatters: Probabilistic payment is one of the standing answers to per-request fees that are smaller than settlement cost, a problem x402 and MPP face whenever an agent buys thousands of cheap API calls.

entries.title: The Case Against Micropayments
entries.summary: Argues from pricing history that people prefer flat-rate and bundled pricing over metered charges, and that the mental cost of deciding on each tiny payment is the main obstacle to micropayments, not the technology.
entries.whyItMatters: The classic objection to pay-per-use pricing; agent payments may sidestep it because software, not a person, makes each spending decision, which is the core bet behind x402 and MPP.

entries.title: Micropayments for Decentralized Currencies
entries.summary: Adapts probabilistic micropayments to decentralized currencies such as Bitcoin, designing schemes where a payer issues lottery-style tickets and only winning tickets are settled on chain, with protections against a payer who double-spends the escrow.
entries.whyItMatters: Links the 1990s micropayment literature to blockchain settlement, the setting in which x402 operates and in which MPP offers on-chain payment methods.

entries.title: The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments
entries.summary: The white paper (draft version 0.5.9.2, dated 2016-01-14) for a network of bidirectional payment channels in which transfers happen off chain and are routed across channels with hashed timelock contracts, so only channel opening and closing touch the blockchain.
entries.whyItMatters: Payment channels are the main route to cheap, fast repeated payments; the deferred and session schemes discussed for x402 and MPP inherit the channel model this paper popularized.

entries.title: Sprites and State Channels: Payment Networks that Go Faster than Lightning
entries.summary: Proposes Sprites, a payment channel construction for smart-contract chains that cuts the worst-case time collateral is locked along a multi-hop route and supports partial deposits and withdrawals without closing the channel. It also gives a modular treatment of general state channels.
entries.whyItMatters: A key reference for channel designs on Ethereum-style chains, where x402 settles; it explains the collateral and dispute costs any channel-based agent payment scheme must budget for.

entries.title: Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments
entries.summary: Introduces blind signatures, where a signer signs a message without seeing it, and uses them to build payments that the bank can verify but cannot link back to the payer.
entries.whyItMatters: The origin of private digital cash; it frames the privacy trade-off in agent payments, where x402 settles on public ledgers and card-based agent payments expose purchase data to the networks.

entries.title: Chip and PIN is Broken
entries.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2010
entries.summary: Shows a man-in-the-middle attack on EMV chip cards in which a device between card and terminal makes the terminal believe the PIN was verified while the card believes signature verification was used, so a stolen card works with any PIN.
entries.whyItMatters: A reminder that card security fails at the seams between parties that each see half the transaction; agent payment schemes add another party, the agent, between cardholder and merchant.

entries.title: Verified by Visa and MasterCard SecureCode: Or, How Not to Design Authentication
entries.venue: Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2010, LNCS
entries.summary: Criticizes the original 3-D Secure schemes (Verified by Visa and MasterCard SecureCode) for training users to enter passwords into unverifiable inline frames, shifting liability onto cardholders, and weakening security in the name of convenience.
entries.whyItMatters: 3-D Secure is the existing step-up and liability mechanism that card-based agent payments build on or bypass; this paper explains why authentication that users cannot verify fails.

entries.title: Chip and Skim: Cloning EMV Cards with the Pre-play Attack
entries.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2014
entries.summary: Finds that many EMV terminals and ATMs generate weak or predictable "unpredictable numbers", which lets an attacker who briefly accesses a card harvest authorization cryptograms in advance and replay them later as if the card were present (the pre-play attack).
entries.whyItMatters: Replay of pre-computed authorizations is the same failure class that agent payment specs try to block with nonces, timestamps and per-request signatures, as in Visa TAP signatures and network tokens.

entries.title: The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify
entries.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2021
entries.summary: Builds a Tamarin model of the EMV contactless protocol and finds that unauthenticated card data lets an attacker bypass the PIN for high-value Visa contactless payments; the authors propose and verify fixes that terminals can deploy.
entries.whyItMatters: The method, formal modeling of a payment network protocol that exposes a deployable attack, is what recent work applies to agent payment specs; it also shows how fragile unauthenticated fields are.

entries.title: Card Brand Mixup Attack: Bypassing the PIN in non-Visa Cards by Using Them for Visa Transactions
entries.summary: Shows that an attacker can make a terminal treat a Mastercard contactless card as a Visa card, routing the transaction so that the earlier Visa PIN bypass applies; the authors demonstrated it with an Android app in real transactions.
entries.whyItMatters: A mismatch between card brand and network routing breaks assumptions on both sides; agent payment designs that span Visa and Mastercard credentials must bind the brand and network explicitly.

entries.title: Practical EMV Relay Protection
entries.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022
entries.summary: Analyzes relay attacks on contactless EMV, including a relay of Apple Pay transit transactions to locked iPhones, and proposes a relay protection protocol with a formal proof that would fit within existing EMV deployments.
entries.whyItMatters: Relay is the card-present version of an agent acting far from the cardholder; the paper shows why binding a payment to its context, not just to valid credentials, matters.

entries.title: Provable Security Analysis of FIDO2
entries.summary: Gives the first provable-security analysis of FIDO2, covering WebAuthn and the CTAP2 authenticator protocol; it proves security properties of WebAuthn, finds weaknesses in CTAP2 and proposes a stronger replacement.
entries.whyItMatters: Passkey and FIDO-based consent is how card networks propose to confirm a cardholder before an agent pays; this paper pins down what the underlying protocol does and does not guarantee.

entries.title: Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously
entries.summary: Presents Privacy Pass, in which a client solves one challenge, receives blindly signed tokens, and redeems them later to skip further challenges without the server linking redemptions to issuance.
entries.whyItMatters: Privacy Pass is the earlier anonymous-token approach to telling trusted clients from bots; Visa TAP instead identifies agents with signed HTTP messages, and comparing the two shows the trade between accountability and privacy.

entries.title: FP-Inconsistent: Measurement and Analysis of Fingerprint Inconsistencies in Evasive Bot Traffic
entries.summary: Buys traffic from 20 bot services against a honey site protected by two commercial anti-bot products and finds that about half the requests evade detection by altering browser fingerprints; inconsistencies among altered attributes then help detect them.
entries.whyItMatters: Measures how weak fingerprint-based bot detection is, which is the problem Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay address by having trusted agents sign their requests instead of hiding as browsers.

entries.title: Cooperation among Competitors: Some Economics of Payment Card Associations
entries.summary: Models a payment card association in which issuers and acquirers cooperate on a network but compete for cardholders and merchants, and studies how the interchange fee balances use and acceptance of cards.
entries.whyItMatters: Interchange is the economic engine that card-based agent payments inherit; the paper explains why networks set fees on one side to grow the other, which shapes who pays for agent checkout.

entries.title: Platform Competition in Two-Sided Markets
entries.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 1(4)
entries.summary: Builds the standard model of competition between two-sided platforms that must attract both buyers and sellers, showing how price structure, not just price level, determines adoption, with payment cards as a leading example.
entries.whyItMatters: Every agentic checkout protocol is a two-sided platform bet; this model explains the subsidy and fee choices behind merchant and agent adoption of ACP, UCP and card network programs.

entries.title: Governing AI Agents
entries.summary: Uses the economics of principal-agent problems and the common law of agency to analyze AI agents, identifying problems of information asymmetry, discretionary authority and loyalty, and argues that incentives, monitoring and enforcement work poorly for agents acting at machine speed and scale.
entries.whyItMatters: Frames delegated purchasing in legal terms, which matters for the mandate and consent records that AP2, Agent Pay and the other protocols produce as evidence of authority.

entries.title: AI Agents and the Law
entries.venue: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2025)
entries.summary: Compares technical and legal ideas of agency, linking implied authority in agency law to value alignment in AI, and argues that computer science has under-theorized the agent's loyalty to its principal and its dealings with third parties.
entries.whyItMatters: Agent payments put third parties (merchants, networks) in contact with an agent; the paper explains which legal duties may attach and why protocols record what the user actually authorized.

entries.title: AI Agents in Payments: Applications, Risks and Regulations
entries.summary: Defines agentic payments as transactions started and completed by AI agents, sets out how they work across retail, e-commerce and decentralized finance, and classifies their technical, legal and societal risks, including liability gaps and regulatory non-compliance.
entries.whyItMatters: One of the few peer-reviewed legal analyses aimed at agent payments specifically, useful for the compliance and liability questions every protocol in the atlas leaves to implementers.

entries.title: Bonded Recourse for Smart-Contract Settlement of Compensable Agent Side Effects
entries.summary: Designs Recourse, a set of smart contracts that binds each agent action to its scope, recovery plan, evidence, payout and collateral, so residual harm from a permitted action that fails can be settled through an optimistic oracle or arbitration. The authors deploy it on Base Sepolia and report less uncompensated harm than authorization-only baselines; the arXiv comment says it was accepted at IEEE BCCA 2026, not yet confirmed in proceedings.
entries.whyItMatters: Adds the after-the-fact remedy that payment and identity protocols lack; it pairs naturally with ERC-8004 reputation and on-chain settlement used by x402.

entries.title: Underwriting the Agent Economy: The Blueprint for an AI Insurance Stack
entries.summary: Argues that AI agent risk is mostly unpriced or excluded in current insurance lines and lays out an eight-part insurance stack, from incident data and catastrophe modeling to standards, pricing and claims, needed for large affirmative coverage by 2030.
entries.whyItMatters: Insurance is a likely backstop for agent purchasing errors that card chargebacks and stablecoin settlement do not cover; the report sketches what insurers would need from protocol logs and standards.

entries.title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
entries.summary: A Cooperative AI Foundation technical report that sorts risks from interacting AI agents into three failure modes (miscoordination, conflict and collusion) and seven risk factors such as information asymmetry, network effects and commitment problems.
entries.whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent commerce is a multi-agent system; the taxonomy names the market failures, such as collusion between buyer and seller agents, that payment protocols alone cannot prevent.
